loadSignals.summary: Installs the global Signal object of the TC39 Signals proposal, which @xaendar/core is built on.
loadSignals.description:
The function defines globalThis.Signal, with Signal.State, Signal.Computed and the Signal.subtle namespace: a polyfill of the TC39 Signals proposal. The signals of @xaendar/core/signals, such as signal(), wrap these classes, and @xaendar/core reads Signal.subtle as soon as its modules are evaluated: the call must come before any of them is loaded.

The global object is defined only when globalThis.Signal does not exist yet: a second call, or a Signal installed by another library, leaves it as it is. The devMode option, instead, is applied at every call.

The type declarations of the package declare the global Signal too: once a file of the project imports @xaendar/signals, TypeScript knows Signal in every file.

members.devMode:
Whether the polyfill runs in dev mode. Defaults to false.

In dev mode it logs in the console the errors thrown inside the callbacks of computed signals, the notify callbacks of watchers, the watched and unwatched callbacks and the functions run by Signal.subtle.untrack(), before rethrowing them as usual. It also warns, with a stack trace, about the invalid state transitions of computed signals and watchers.

The option is applied at every call, even when the global object is already installed: a later call without it turns dev mode off.

entryPoint.title: Calling it in the entry point
entryPoint.body: Call it in the entry point of the application, then load the modules using @xaendar/core with await import(): the static imports of a module are evaluated before its body, even when they are written after the call. The main.ts created by xd new does it.

missing.title: When it has not run yet
missing.body: A module of @xaendar/core evaluated before the call reads a Signal that does not exist, and the application stops before rendering anything:

specs.title: In specs
specs.body: xd test installs the global object before every spec file. A project running Vitest by itself does the same with a setup file, listed in the setupFiles of its configuration.

SignalOptions.summary: The options of a signal: how a new value is compared with the current one, and what runs when the signal starts and stops being watched.
SignalOptions.description:
The options are taken by Signal.State and by signal(), and, together with transform and alias, by the inputs declared with @Property. Signal.Computed and computed() take only equals.

Every callback is called with the signal as this: the Signal.State or the Signal.Computed itself, also when the signal was created by signal() or computed(), whose functions wrap it. An arrow function has no this of its own: use a method to read it.

members.equals:
Decides whether a new value is equal to the current one. It is called with the signal as this, the current value and the new one, and returns true when they are equal. Defaults to Object.is: for objects and arrays, that means identity, not content. Its type is SignalEqual.

On a Signal.State, set() calls it first: when it returns true, the new value is discarded and nobody is notified. An exception it throws escapes from set(), and the value does not change.

On a Signal.Computed, it compares each new result with the cached one: when it returns true, the cached result is kept, and the computed signals reading it are not evaluated again because of it. It is not called for the first result, nor after an evaluation that threw. An exception it throws is cached as the result, like one thrown by the callback.
members.watched:
Called with the signal as this when the signal gets its first sink: a watcher watching it, or a computed signal reading it, such as the one an effect or a template binding runs in. It is the place to start whatever feeds the signal: a timer, a subscription, an event listener. A read outside of any computed signal does not count.

Signals are frozen while it runs: reading or writing one throws, so the writes have to be deferred. Only a Signal.State calls it: Signal.Computed does not support the option.

A computed signal counts as a sink only while it is live: while a watcher watches it, directly or through other computed signals. Reading the signal in a computed signal that nothing watches does not call watched. A live computed signal stays a sink of the signals it reads from one evaluation to the next, so watched runs once, not at each evaluation.
members.unwatched:
Called with the signal as this when the signal loses its last sink: the last watcher watching it stops watching it, or the last computed signal reading it loses its own last sink or is evaluated again without reading it. It is the place to stop what watched started.

As for watched, signals are frozen while it runs, and only a Signal.State calls it.

equality.title: Comparing by content
equality.body: A custom equals lets a new object with the same content, or the same identity for the application, replace the current one without notifying anybody.

source.title: Starting and stopping what feeds a signal
source.body: watched starts a timer when something starts depending on the clock, and unwatched stops it when nothing does any more. A template binding reading the clock is evaluated again at every tick, but it stays a sink of the clock: each callback runs once, when the binding is created and when it is removed.

SignalEqual.summary: The type of the equals option of a signal: a function telling whether a new value is equal to the current one.
SignalEqual.description:
A function of this type is called with the signal as this, the current value and the new one, and returns true when the two are equal: the new value is then not a change. SignalOptions describes when a state and a computed signal call it, and what happens when it throws.

The two values are typed any, whatever T is: annotate the parameters to have them checked.

members.this: The signal comparing the values: the Signal.State or the Signal.Computed itself, also for the signals created by signal() and computed(). Only a regular function receives it: an arrow function keeps the this of the code around it.
members.t: The current value: the one the state holds, or the result the computed signal has cached.
members.t2: The new value: the one passed to set(), or the new result of the computed signal.

reusable.title: A reusable comparison
reusable.body: Declaring the function with its type lets several signals share it. The annotations of the parameters are what checks the values.

ExtractSignalType.summary: The type of the value held by a Signal.State type.
ExtractSignalType.description:
For a type assignable to Signal.State<T>, it is T; for any other type, it is never. The Signal type of @xaendar/core/signals, returned by signal(), extends Signal.State, so it works on it too.

A read-only signal has no set(), so it is not a Signal.State: Signal.Computed, Computed and InputSignal give never. A union of states gives the union of their value types.

deriving.title: Taking a type from a signal
deriving.body: The type of the value can be taken from the signal holding it, instead of being written again.

Signal.State.summary: A writable signal: it holds a value, and tells the computed signals and the watchers depending on it when the value changes.
Signal.State.description:
The class is installed on the global Signal object by loadSignals(), and implements the Signal.State of the TC39 Signals proposal. signal() creates one and wraps it in a function, which is what application code uses. The class itself is needed with Signal.subtle, which works on the instances only.

A state is linked to its sinks: the watchers watching it, and the live computed signals, the ones a watcher watches directly or through other computed signals, that read it in their last evaluation. A change marks those computed signals stale and notifies the watchers, synchronously, inside set(); the computed signals are evaluated again only when they are read.

members.initialValue: The value the state holds until set() stores a different one. It also gives T its type, unless the type is passed explicitly, as in new Signal.State<string | null>(null).
members.options: How the values are compared, and what runs when the state starts and stops being watched: equals, watched and unwatched, described in SignalOptions. Without options, the values are compared with Object.is.
members.get:
Returns the current value. Inside the evaluation of a computed signal, such as the callback of a Signal.Computed, an effect or a template binding, it also records the state as a source of that computed signal, which is marked stale when the state changes. Outside of any evaluation, or inside Signal.subtle.untrack(), it is a plain read.

It throws Cannot get value while signals are frozen inside the notify callback of a watcher and inside watched and unwatched.
members.set:
Replaces the value, unless equals, Object.is by default, says that the new value equals the current one: then the call does nothing. Otherwise it stores the value and, synchronously, marks stale the computed signals that read the state and the ones depending on them, and calls the notify callback of the watchers watching the state, or a computed signal that becomes stale, unless they already notified since their last watch(). No computed signal is evaluated: each one is evaluated again the next time it is read.

It throws Cannot set value while signals are frozen inside notify, watched and unwatched. An exception thrown by equals or by a notify callback escapes from set(): in the first case the value is still the old one, in the second the new one is already stored.

direct.title: Using a state directly
direct.body: A state is read with get() and written with set(). A watcher watching it is notified before set() returns, and an equal value notifies nobody.

wrapper.title: The function returned by signal() is not a state
wrapper.body: signal() keeps its Signal.State private, and returns a function exposing its get() and set(). The type of that function extends Signal.State, so passing it to a watcher or to Signal.subtle type-checks, but throws at run time: create the state with new Signal.State() when those APIs need it.

Signal.Computed.summary: A read-only signal whose value is derived from other signals: evaluated lazily, it records the signals it reads as its sources.
Signal.Computed.description:
The class is installed on the global Signal object by loadSignals(), and implements the Signal.Computed of the TC39 Signals proposal. computed() creates one and wraps it in a function; effect() and the template bindings run their code in one, watched by a Signal.subtle.Watcher.

Creating it runs nothing: the callback runs at the first get(). Each evaluation records the signals the callback reads as the sources of the computed signal, forgetting the ones of the previous evaluation, so a signal read only in a branch that was not taken is not a source. When a source changes, the computed signal is marked stale, and evaluated again by the next read.

The value is cached only while the computed signal has a sink: a watcher watching it, or another computed signal reading it. Without sinks, every get() runs the callback again.

members.callback:
The function deriving the value. It is called with the computed signal as this: inside a regular function, this is the Signal.Computed, while an arrow function keeps the this of the code around it. The signals it reads become the sources of the computed signal, except the ones read inside Signal.subtle.untrack().

Keep it pure: it runs when the value is read, as many times as needed, or never. A result it returns is compared with the cached one by equals; an exception it throws is cached, and every get() rethrows it until an evaluation succeeds.
members.options: Only equals, which compares each new result with the cached one: see SignalOptions. Defaults to Object.is. watched and unwatched are not supported: TypeScript rejects them, and they would be ignored.
members.get:
Returns the value, evaluating the callback first when needed: at the first read, when a source has changed since the last evaluation, and at every read while the computed signal has no sinks. When it is stale only because a computed signal it reads may have changed, that one is evaluated first, and this one only if the result of that one changed: a computed signal is evaluated at most once per change, after the ones it depends on.

Like Signal.State, inside the evaluation of another computed signal it records itself as a source of that one.

It throws the exception cached by the last evaluation, Circular dependency detected while computing a Computed signal when the callback reads the computed signal itself, directly or through other computed signals, and Cannot get value of a Computed signal while the global state is frozen inside notify, watched and unwatched.

direct.title: Using a computed signal directly
direct.body: The callback runs at the first read, which records its sources. With a sink, here a watcher, the value is cached until a source changes, and the change only marks it stale: the next read evaluates it again.

Signal.subtle.summary: The low-level API of the signals: watchers, reads without tracking, and the introspection of the graph of signals.
Signal.subtle.description:
The namespace is installed on the global Signal object by loadSignals(), and implements the Signal.subtle of the TC39 Signals proposal: the primitives effects and frameworks are built on. Application code rarely needs it: effect() combines a Signal.Computed with a Watcher, and untracked is Signal.subtle.untrack.

The watchers and the introspection functions work on the instances of Signal.State and Signal.Computed, not on the functions returned by signal() and computed(): passing one of those type-checks, because their types extend the classes, but throws at run time.

Unlike the proposal, the namespace has no watched and unwatched symbols: the callbacks are passed to a state as plain options, described in SignalOptions.

members.Watcher:
The class of the watchers: a watcher is told, synchronously, that the signals it watches may have changed. new Signal.subtle.Watcher(notify) creates one watching nothing, and watch() adds signals to it.

notify is called with the watcher as this, inside the set() that changes a watched state, or that makes a watched computed signal stale. Signals are frozen while it runs: reading or writing one, and calling watch() or unwatch(), throws, so it can only schedule the work, for example with queueMicrotask. An exception it throws escapes from that set().

A watcher notifies once, then waits: the next changes do not call notify until watch() re-arms it, so the work it schedules runs once however many changes arrive in the meantime. That work reads the stale computed signals with getPending(), then calls watch() with no arguments to be notified again, as effect() does.
members.untrack:
Runs fn and returns its result, without recording the signals it reads as sources of the computed signal being evaluated. Only the reads inside fn are not tracked: the same signal read before or after the call is tracked as usual. A computed signal read inside fn still records its own sources, but is not a source of the outer one.

It is the untracked of @xaendar/core/signals. It does not unfreeze the signals: inside notify, watched and unwatched, its reads throw too. An exception thrown by fn escapes, after being logged in dev mode.
members.currentComputed: Returns the computed signal being evaluated, the one the reads are recorded in, or null outside of any evaluation and inside untrack(). Inside an effect or a template binding, it is the computed signal they run in.
members.introspectSources: Returns the sources of a node, in the order they were first read. For a computed signal, the signals its last evaluation read: none before the first one. For a watcher, the signals it watches. The array is a copy: changing it changes nothing.
members.introspectSinks: Returns the sinks of a signal: the watchers watching it, and the live computed signals that read it in their last evaluation: a computed signal that nothing watches is not a sink. A computed signal leaves the sinks of the sources it no longer reads when it is evaluated again, and of all its sources when it loses its last sink. The array is a copy.
members.hasSources: Whether introspectSources(node) is not empty. It is false for a computed signal not evaluated yet, or whose last evaluation read no signal, and for a watcher watching nothing.
members.hasSinks: Whether introspectSinks(signal) is not empty: whether a watcher watches the signal, or a computed signal read it in its last evaluation. A state runs its watched callback when this becomes true, and its unwatched callback when it becomes false again.
members.Watcher.prototype.watch:
Adds signals to the watcher. The watcher becomes a sink of each of them, and a computed signal getting its first sink links to its sources, so that a change of any of them reaches the watcher. A state getting its first sink runs its watched callback.

Watching a computed signal does not evaluate it, and a computed signal never evaluated has no sources: read it once with get(), or no change will ever be notified.

It throws Cannot watch a signal that is already being watched for a signal the watcher already watches, after adding the signals before it, and Cannot watch signals while frozen inside notify, watched and unwatched. Called with no signals, it adds nothing and re-arms the watcher after a notification, so that the next change notifies it again: effect() calls it so after each run.
members.Watcher.prototype.unwatch:
Removes signals from the watcher. A computed signal losing its last sink leaves the sinks of its sources, recursively, and a state losing its last sink runs its unwatched callback. To stop watching everything, pass the sources of the watcher: watcher.unwatch(...Signal.subtle.introspectSources(watcher)).

It throws Cannot unwatch a signal that is not being watched for a signal the watcher does not watch, after removing the signals before it, and Cannot unwatch signals while frozen inside notify, watched and unwatched.
members.Watcher.prototype.getPending: Returns the computed signals the watcher watches that are stale: the ones whose sources changed, or may have changed, since their last evaluation. The work scheduled by notify reads them with get(), which evaluates them again. States are never pending, and neither are the computed signals the watcher reaches only through other ones.

effect.title: An effect built by hand
effect.body: A Signal.Computed runs the code and records what it reads; a watcher schedules a new evaluation when any of it changes. This is, in essence, what effect() does: use that in application code.

introspection.title: Inspecting the graph
introspection.body: Evaluating a computed signal links it to its sources, in both directions; losing its last sink unlinks it again.

frozen.title: Signals are frozen in the callbacks
frozen.body: While notify, watched or unwatched run, the graph is being updated and every signal is frozen. Reading or writing a signal, or changing what a watcher watches, throws one of these errors. Schedule the work instead: queueMicrotask, a timer, an event.
